transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 1:18
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (CISO, Quarry), Diego Marquez (Head Infra), Ellen Park (Cloud Security), Tom Nguyen (Network)

Summary:
Quick security deep-dive for Quarry's planned private deployment (on-prem + VPC peering). Focus areas: network isolation, ingress/egress control, firewalling, audit logs, KMS integration, SOC2 scope. Action items and follow-ups captured at end.

Topics:
- High-level architecture and trust boundaries
- Ingress/egress patterns and egress proxies/NAT
- Firewalling: segmentation, microseg, L4 vs L7
- Identity: SSO/SAML, RBAC mapping, least privilege
- Auditability: audit logs, log retention, tamper-evidence
- Encryption: KMS vs HSM, key rotation, envelope encryption
- Compliance: SOC2/ISO implications for private deployment

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Meyers: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um today we wanted to walk through the security boundaries for the private deployment that Quarry is considering. Priya and Liam are with me from the SE team.
[00:18] Aisha Rahman: thanks Jordan. quick bit of context: we have a compliance timeline — SOC 2 readiness in Q2, and a handful of high-sensitivity workloads that must stay on-prem or in our private colo racks. so network isolation is a must.
[00:35] Priya Desai: totally understood. so from Redwood's side we support a private control plane + on-prem runtime; most customers either run in a VPC with VPC peering or air-gapped on-prem. for the network bits, are you planning egress to external model registries or is everything internal?
[00:52] Diego Marquez: majority internal, but we will need occasional outbound for base-image pulls, updates, and telemetry to a limited set of endpoints. we'd like to minimize blast radius and strictly allow only whitelisted egress.
[01:08] Liam O'Connor: ok noted. typical pattern we recommend is an egress proxy/NAT that keeps DNS and TLS whitelisted endpoints and mTLS where possible. side note: our runtime supports mutual TLS to the control plane if you choose the managed control plane model.
[01:29] Tom Nguyen: couple quick Qs — where does the KV cache live in the private runtime? is that in-memory on the inference servers or an external store? i've seen it called key-v cache in some docs and want to make sure we know the persistence semantics.
[01:46] Priya Desai: good question. the KV cache is in-memory on the inference nodes for latency reasons; checkpointing is optional and you can configure sticky cache affinity. persistent state is only for model artifacts in the artifact store. apologies if the docs said key-v — that is a common speech->text artifact.
[02:05] Aisha Rahman: on the SOC 2 front we need audit trails for who accessed what model and when. does Redwood emit token-level audit logs or user-principal logs that we can ship to our SIEM?
[02:22] Jordan Meyers: we can emit both. Redwood Private can push structured audit events to your syslog/stack or to cloud logging endpoints. token-level traces are available but we recommend consuming the per-request metadata — user principal, model id, route, and outcome. klaus, we have a sample log schema in the private docs — will share.
[02:45] Ellen Park: it's important that logs are immutable and retention is configurable — we have legal retention of 7 years on certain ML telemetry. can we get WORM/immutable mode or integration to our archival HSM?
[03:01] Priya Desai: we don't provide WORM storage natively, but we support write-once-side policies at the storage layer (e.g., S3 Object Lock or your on-prem archive appliance). for HSMs we support external KMS wrappers so keys are never in the clear.
[03:20] Diego Marquez: about the KMS — we're evaluating AWS KMS vs Thales HSM in our colo. what's the integration pattern? do you require a specific provider?
[03:33] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Private can integrate with customer KMS via standard APIs. you can bring AWS KMS, an on-prem HSM, or a Vault cluster. the runtime supports envelope encryption and a local key-encryption-key (KEK) flow. key rotation is supported but needs coordination for cached token/key lifetimes.
[03:53] Tom Nguyen: sounds good. for firewalling: we have a north-south perimeter firewall and internal ACLs. do you recommend putting inference nodes in a separate VLAN with a hardened bastion for management?
[04:07] Priya Desai: yes that's our recommended pattern. segregate inference nodes into isolated subnets, use a management bastion with jump host + session recording for admin ops, and only allow control-plane egress to the minimal IPs.
[04:24] Aisha Rahman: how is SSO handled? our audit requires SAML-based SSO and SCIM provisioning.
[04:31] Jordan Meyers: Redwood supports SAML 2.0 and SCIM provisioning to sync groups. RBAC maps can be translated from your IdP groups into Redwood roles — we can provide a mapping template.
[04:45] Diego Marquez: and RBAC granularity? can we restrict who can deploy models vs who can call endpoints?
[04:51] Priya Desai: yes, roles are split: deployer, operator, auditor, consumer. deploy privileges are separate from runtime invocation. invocation can also be restricted to service accounts that we issue or that you manage.
[05:05] Tom Nguyen: what about egress controls on a per-route basis? we have data residency rules that certain requests must never leave EU. can we pin those to local regions or on-prem only?
[05:18] Liam O'Connor: yes, you can pin routes and model variants to physical locations. the routing policy can fallback to a lower-capacity local model or deny outright. we also support region tags and SLOs — if a call would violate residency we can fail closed.
[05:36] Aisha Rahman: we need a crisp answer for our auditors: what artifacts will Redwood share for SOC 2 evidence?
[05:44] Jordan Meyers: we can provide control evidence: architecture diagrams, network ACL lists, sample audit logs, SOC 2 related controls mapping for the private deployment. for hosted endpoints we have third-party SOC 2 reports; for private deployed software we provide the compliance mapping and operational runbooks.
[06:03] Diego Marquez: on the network side we want to talk about L4 vs L7 firewalling. our threat team prefers L7 inspection for anomaly detection, but performance for token-level inference is a concern. any guidance?
[06:18] Priya Desai: tradeoff is throughput versus deep inspection. for inference traffic we recommend L4 with strict allow lists and mTLS; L7 (deep packet inspection) can be used at the edge — e.g., ingress to the egress proxy — but avoid inline L7 on the inference path.
[06:36] Tom Nguyen: noted. what about running the control plane locally vs using Redwood's managed control plane?
[06:42] Liam O'Connor: if you host the control plane on-prem you get full control of metadata and keys. the managed control plane is easier but requires tight peering and some trust. many large banks run the control plane in a customer VPC with private link to Redwood services.
[06:58] Aisha Rahman: we're leaning to hosting locally or colocating the control plane in our VPC — to satisfy auditors. what happens to telemetry and usage metrics in that case?
[07:08] Jordan Meyers: telemetry can be kept local. we have an offline metrics exporter that will push to your metrics backend (Prometheus/Grafana) without egressing raw traces to Redwood. there are tradeoffs around feature telemetry but core metrics are preserved.
[07:22] Diego Marquez: latency question: if we run everything on-prem and enable KV cache affinity and local artifact store, what kind of p99 token latency should we expect for a medium-sized model? this is high-level but helps sizing.
[07:36] Priya Desai: with 4xA100 and local storage you're looking at sub-60ms token generation p95 in typical configs; p99 depends on sequencing and batch behavior. our benchmark harness can simulate your sequence length distribution. we'll offer a benchmark run.
[07:53] Ellen Park: for compliance we need tamper-resistant audit logs. do you support signing of logs or an append-only ledger?
[08:01] Liam O'Connor: we don't ship a blockchain ledger but we support signing of log batches with customer KMS and push to your archival store. you can also stream to a SIEM and enable write-only retention policies.
[08:15] Aisha Rahman: ok can you walk quickly through a hardened deployment diagram?
[08:20] Priya Desai: sure — I'll describe verbally and attach the diagram after. inbound requests hit an ingress proxy in the DMZ that only accepts TLS from your application subnets, the proxy forwards to the egress-filtered inference subnet. inference nodes sit in a private VLAN with no direct internet. management plane goes through a bastion with recorded sessions. keys are in the KMS/HSM, audit logs stream to your SIEM, and backups go to immutable archive.
[08:47] Diego Marquez: do you support SR-IOV or NIC passthrough for high-performance inference boxes in colo? we may have specialized NICs for RDMA clusters.
[08:58] Liam O'Connor: that's mostly at the hypervisor/container runtime level — Redwood's runtime can operate on bare metal or VMs. SR-IOV is supported as long as the host environment exposes the device; we don't require a particular NIC vendor.
[09:14] Tom Nguyen: any gotchas on key rotation? we rotate monthly internally and need to ensure cached sessions don't break.
[09:21] Priya Desai: rotation is smooth if you use envelope encryption; rotate the key-encrypting key (KEK) and the runtime will rewrap new artifacts. for cached in-memory keys, we recommend a short cache TTL and coordinated rotation windows. we'll provide a rotation runbook.
[09:35] Aisha Rahman: are there specific tests we should run during PoC to validate compliance boundaries?
[09:41] Jordan Meyers: yes — we recommend: egress whitelisting test, failure-mode test for residency (simulate a model travel to another region and ensure deny), role-mismatch test (attempt deploy with low-priv user), log integrity test (write logs and attempt to modify), and key-rotation consumption test.
[09:58] Diego Marquez: when you say deny, is there an explicit policy engine? or is it a config flag?
[10:04] Liam O'Connor: it's policy-driven; we expose route policies that you can set to allow/deny/fail-closed and you can tag resources with residency constraints.
[10:16] Tom Nguyen: noise in transcription — sorry — quick question on session recording for admin ops: can we integrate recordings into our SecOps VRM?
[10:24] Priya Desai: we can export recording artifacts to your storage and the session metadata to your VRM. format is standard mp4 + audit json.
[10:32] Aisha Rahman: auditors will ask about separation of duties — can Redwood limit who can see the plaintext inference outputs if those outputs are considered sensitive?
[10:41] Jordan Meyers: yes — access controls can be enforced at the route level. we can redact outputs in logs or mask them. also you can have outputs encrypted with a tenant key so only downstream consumers with access can decrypt.
[10:55] Diego Marquez: would there be any additional certifications needed if we host? like does Redwood provide guidance for ISO 27001 mapping for private deployments?
[11:03] Liam O'Connor: we have an ISO control mapping doc that maps our platform capabilities to ISO controls. for private deployments we'll provide the mapping and recommended operational controls you'd need to own.
[11:15] Tom Nguyen: got it. do you collect any PII by default in telemetry? we need to ensure PII is never captured.
[11:21] Priya Desai: telemetry can be configured to exclude PII. by default we don't capture raw user content in managed logs for private deployments unless you enable it for debugging; we can turn that off.
[11:34] Aisha Rahman: ok let's capture next steps.
[11:38] Jordan Meyers: action items: Priya will run a benchmark with the config we discussed; Tom will send firewall rulebook; Ellen will confirm KMS choice; Jordan will send a pricing / commitment ballpark and compliance artifacts. we'll reconvene after you've had a chance to review the docs and benchmark.
[11:56] Diego Marquez: quick operational question — how are OS security updates handled on inference nodes? automatic or customer-managed?
[12:04] Liam O'Connor: depends on deployment mode. in customer-managed on-prem the customer controls patching; we provide recommended images and an upgrade runbook. in Redwood-managed dedicated infra we handle patch rollouts in maintenance windows.
[12:18] Tom Nguyen: thanks. any known performance impacts when TLS is terminated at the egress proxy vs passthrough?
[12:24] Priya Desai: terminating TLS at the proxy can add small CPU overhead but allows for inspection and SNI routing; passthrough is cheaper but less flexible. if you're worried about CPU, use L4 passthrough with mTLS.
[12:38] Aisha Rahman: are there any red-team concerns? i.e., if someone gets lateral access, what safeguards prevent exfil of model weights or logs?
[12:47] Jordan Meyers: recommended controls: network segmentation, appliance-based DLP at egress, encrypt-at-rest with customer keys, and minimal service accounts for artifact access. also lock down model artifact store with ACLs.
[13:02] Diego Marquez: cliff notes for auditors — can you produce a one-page controls summary we can hand to the SOC auditor?
[13:09] Jordan Meyers: yes will include a one-page controls summary: network segregation, key management, audit logging, RBAC, SSO, and retention policies.
[13:20] Ellen Park: please include potential gaps that remain customer-owned. auditors always ask where responsibility splits.
[13:26] Priya Desai: absolutely — we'll include a responsibility matrix (RACI-esque).
[13:32] Tom Nguyen: do you have a recommended test harness for egress whitelisting? we'd like reproducible tests.
[13:40] Liam O'Connor: yes, we'll share a small tool that simulates outbound DNS/TLS to endpoints and verifies allowlist behavior.
[13:49] Aisha Rahman: okay time check, are there any showstoppers we've heard so far?
[13:54] Diego Marquez: none on our side. just need the KMS choice clarified and some init bench numbers.
[14:00] Jordan Meyers: quick note — we also support per-tenant keystores if you want keys physically separated. that helps with strict separation.
[14:08] Ellen Park: good. for timeline: we want a PoC in Jan, and SOC 2 purple-team in Q2. can Redwood commit to the PoC support?
[14:18] Jordan Meyers: yes, we'll do a PoC with SE support and a bench plan.
[14:23] Priya Desai: we'll also include the security runbook and the network diagram.
[14:28] Aisha Rahman: one last: any legal / procurement docs we should sign to proceed? NDA is okay, but also a data processing addendum?
[14:35] Jordan Meyers: standard NDA is fine; for private deployments we'll present a Data Processing Addendum and a security addendum covering handling of customer keys and data.
[14:44] Diego Marquez: great — thanks everyone.

[end of meeting notes]
